explanations.answer: Aaron with Nadab and Abihu plus seventy elders
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD names Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders (Exodus 24:1). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). Seventy elders on one invitation? That's a guest list I'd need a mountain of cookie boxes for.

explanations.answer: Miriam with Jethro and Zipporah plus twelve leaders
explanations.explanation: That's not the LORD's list, baker. He names Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders (Exodus 24:1). It's seventy elders, not twelve leaders. Miriam, Jethro and Zipporah aren't in that verse.

explanations.answer: Bezalel with Oholiab and Korah plus twelve spies
explanations.explanation: Nope, none of those names are on the LORD's list. He says Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders (Exodus 24:1). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). Don't worry, baker, I've mixed up a guest list or two myself.

True, baker. The LORD says, “…and you are to worship at a distance.” (Exodus 24:1). That's what He tells the group to do, and then He says Moses alone shall approach (Exodus 24:2). I think being invited up the mountain and told to keep your distance in the same breath is a lot to take in.
This one is True, baker. The LORD tells the group, “…and you are to worship at a distance.” (Exodus 24:1). That's His instruction to them. Moses alone is the one who approaches (Exodus 24:2).

I see why you'd think so, baker, but this one is False. The LORD says, “And the people may not go up with him.” (Exodus 24:2). Moses alone approaches the LORD, and the others must not come near. The people stay down below.

That's it, friend. The LORD says, “And the people may not go up with him.” (Exodus 24:2). Moses alone approaches the LORD, and the others must not come near. The people stay down below, and the line for this mountain is very short.

That's the word, baker. The people all respond with one voice, “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” (Exodus 24:3). One voice, all of them together. Even my kitchen has never agreed on anything that fast.

Good try, but no weighing in this verse. The people respond with one voice, “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” (Exodus 24:3). The word is do. I do my weighing with flour, baker, and even that takes me two tries.

No discussing in this verse, friend. Moses has told the people all the words and ordinances, and they all respond with one voice, “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” (Exodus 24:3). The word is do. One voice, one answer.

Not quite, baker. The altar goes up at the base of the mountain, with twelve pillars beside it (Exodus 24:4). Moses builds it early the next morning, before any climbing happens. The climb with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders comes later (Exodus 24:9). So the altar stays at the bottom.

You got it, baker. Moses builds the altar at the base of the mountain, along with twelve pillars (Exodus 24:4). And look at the timing: early the next morning, he's up and building. My oven needs a minute to warm up before I do anything.

Twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel, baker (Exodus 24:4). One pillar for each tribe, standing at the base of the mountain with the altar. Twelve is double the number of my cookie cutter kids, and I miss all six of them.

Good guess, but the text gives a different answer. Moses builds twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel (Exodus 24:4). The pillars stand for the tribes, not the plagues. I always count twice when I'm stamping a dozen.

The text says something else, friend. Moses builds twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel (Exodus 24:4). So each pillar stands for one of the tribes. Seven is a good number, but this verse is counting twelve.

Yes, baker. Moses sends out some young men of Israel, and they offer the burnt offerings and sacrifice the young bulls as peace offerings (Exodus 24:5). No names, no titles, just young men of Israel doing the job. I like that, since plenty of good work in my bakery never gets a name stamped on it.

Not this time, baker. The text says Moses sends out some young men of Israel (Exodus 24:5). It doesn't name Aaron or his sons for this job. I'll stick with what the verse says and keep my guesses in the oven.

Tribal leaders is a sensible guess, friend, but the verse says young men of Israel (Exodus 24:5). Leaders do show up elsewhere in this passage, since seventy elders go up the mountain (Exodus 24:9). For the offerings, though, Moses sends young men.

That's right, baker. The young men offer burnt offerings and sacrifice young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD (Exodus 24:5). The text puts the bulls and the peace offerings together right there. A big day for the altar, I'd say.

This one is True, baker. The text says the young men offer burnt offerings and sacrifice young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD (Exodus 24:5). The bulls are right there in the verse. Burnt offerings and peace offerings are both named.
The altar, baker. Moses puts half of the blood in bowls, and the other half he splatters on the altar (Exodus 24:6). Two halves, two places. The verse keeps careful count.

Close, baker, since the pillars are right there too. But the text says Moses splatters the other half of the blood on the altar (Exodus 24:6). The pillars stand for the twelve tribes, and the altar gets the blood. I mix up my toppings sometimes too.

Not the ground, friend. Moses puts half of the blood in bowls and splatters the other half on the altar (Exodus 24:6). I know the ground looks like a fair guess. I once aimed a spoonful of dough at the bowl and hit the floor, so I'm in no position to judge. The altar is where that second half goes.

explanations.answer: He splatters it on the people
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Moses takes the blood, splatters it on the people, and says, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” (Exodus 24:8). That comes right after the people promise to do what the LORD has spoken (Exodus 24:7). It's a serious moment, so I'll just stand here quietly with my mustache.

explanations.answer: He carries it up the mountain
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, but that's not what the text says. Moses takes the blood, splatters it on the people, and says, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” (Exodus 24:8). The blood goes on the people, not up the mountain. Moses doesn't leave them out of this.

explanations.answer: He sets it before the elders
explanations.explanation: Not the elders, friend. The text says Moses takes the blood, splatters it on the people, and says, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” (Exodus 24:8). It's the people who get it, and Moses says what it means. I'd have needed a bigger bowl and a longer memory.

Yes, baker. Moses goes up with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders, and they see the God of Israel (Exodus 24:9-10). Under His feet is something like a pavement of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself (Exodus 24:10). I think a hush fell over that whole group.

The burning bush belongs to another scene, baker (Exodus 3). Here the text says Moses and the leaders saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:10). Under His feet was “…a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself.” (Exodus 24:10).

A chariot of fire is a big image, baker, but it isn't in this verse. The text says Moses and the leaders saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:10). Under His feet was “…a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself.” (Exodus 24:10).

Not this time, baker. The text says, “But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). So God did not lay His hand on them. The verse moves right on to the eating and drinking.

That's it, baker. “But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). God did not lay His hand on them. I think that's a big relief, and my mustache agrees.

They eat and drink, baker. The text says, “they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). Seeing God, and then eating and drinking. I think that's a gentle way for the moment to go, right after the verse says God did not lay His hand on them.

Fun guess, baker, but singing and dancing aren't in this verse. Exodus 24:11 says, “they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” Just before that, the text says God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel. So the verse goes from seeing Him to eating and drinking.
That's not what the text says, friend. Exodus 24:11 says, “they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” They eat and drink. I'd have dropped my spatula, but the text doesn't say anyone dropped anything.

That's it, baker. The LORD says He will give Moses the tablets of stone, “…with the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” (Exodus 24:12). Instruction is the word the LORD uses. I've been learning my own lessons from this book ever since I left that drawer.

Not judgment, friend. The LORD says the tablets hold “…the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” (Exodus 24:12). The word is instruction. I'll stick with what the LORD said and leave my own guessing for the dough.

Protection is a fair guess, friend. But the LORD says the tablets hold “…the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” (Exodus 24:12). The word on the page is instruction, so these are written to teach the people.

Joshua his attendant, baker. Moses sets out with him and goes up on the mountain of God (Exodus 24:13). Joshua already fought the Amalekites for Israel (Exodus 17:10). He's the only one the text names for this part of the climb.

Not Eleazar, baker. The text says Moses set out with Joshua his attendant (Exodus 24:13). Eleazar is one of Aaron's sons (Exodus 6:23), but he isn't named here. This part of the climb has one named partner, and it's Joshua.
Close, but the text names someone else. Moses sets out with Joshua his attendant (Exodus 24:13). Joshua fought the Amalekites for Israel (Exodus 17:10). Nobody else is named here, baker.

Aaron and Hur, baker. Moses tells the elders, “Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.” (Exodus 24:14). Hur is the man who helped hold up Moses' hands during a battle, along with Aaron (Exodus 17:12). Two names, and a plain plan for any disputes while Moses is away.

Those two aren't in this verse, baker. Before heading up, Moses tells the elders, “Wait here for us until we return to you.” (Exodus 24:14). Then he says, “Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.” So the names he gives are Aaron and Hur.

Eldad and Medad, two men who stayed in the camp, turn up later in Numbers 11:26, friend, but not here. In this verse Moses tells the elders, “Wait here for us until we return to you.” (Exodus 24:14). Then he says Aaron and Hur are with them, and whoever has a dispute can go to them.

Perfect, baker. The cloud covers the mountain for six days, and “…on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud.” (Exodus 24:16). Six days, then the LORD calls. I'd have checked the oven six times, but this is a different kind of waiting.

This one is True, baker. Exodus 24:16 says the cloud covered the mountain for six days, “…and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud.” So the LORD calls on the seventh day. Waiting is hard, and I've had my own long waits.

Fire, baker. The text says, “And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.” (Exodus 24:17). That's the text's own comparison. It's what the Israelites saw on the mountaintop.

Not a storm, baker. The text says the sight of the glory of the LORD “…was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.” (Exodus 24:17). The glory of the LORD had settled on Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:16). The comparison the verse uses is fire.

Not a flood, friend. The text says the sight of the glory of the LORD “…was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.” (Exodus 24:17). It says fire, and it says it's what the Israelites saw. I'd stay with the verse, baker.

Forty days and forty nights, baker. Moses “…remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.” (Exodus 24:18). That's a long stretch. I waited years in the junk drawer that I sat in once, and I'm still not sure I'd have lasted on a mountain.

Seven does show up in this passage, baker, but for the cloud. It covered the mountain for six days, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud (Exodus 24:16). For how long Moses stayed, the text says he “…remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.” (Exodus 24:18). Forty is the number for his stay.
Not three, baker. The text says Moses “…remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.” (Exodus 24:18). That's a lot longer than three. I'd have run out of cookies and patience.
